passage:
Monday, week one. Vijay wrote one line on the whiteboard: 20 clinics signed up and paying by the last Friday of week six. Aadhya taped a sheet over the old feature wish-list and marked the report date for the advisors in red.
Thursday, week three. Nine clinics had watched a demo and three had paid. A developer asked to start a new settings screen; Vijay pointed at the whiteboard and said it could wait. Aadhya booked another round of calls instead.
Friday, week six. Eleven clinics were paying. Vijay's shoulders dropped, then straightened, and the numbers went to the advisors that same afternoon, short of the target and unedited.

qa.q: How many clinics were paying on the Friday of week six?
What was Vijay probably feeling when sending the numbers on that Friday?
qa.a: Vijay was probably disappointed but steady: the dropped and then straightened shoulders show the letdown, and sending the unedited numbers on time shows resolve.

qa.q: What different approach could the team try if the calls in week three had gone badly, and why?
qa.a: They could look for the root cause by phoning clinics that declined and asking why, because that would show whether to fix the offer or change direction.

qa.q: How might the advisors see the single target and the fixed report date?
qa.a: The advisors get one clear number on a known day, so they can judge the experiment fairly without guessing how it went. 🙂

grounding: The passage shows a team that sets a short fixed period and one measure, freezes other work and reports on a fixed date.

passage:
Rajni ma'am tapped the table with her pen when the young founder said they were trying a few new directions. "A few? Let me tell you about Sahil. Six years ago his team's clinic software was dying. He came to our advisors' meeting with a plan that fitted on one card: six weeks, one measure: by 15 March, twenty clinics would be paying for reminders. If yes, they would rebuild around it. If no, they would think again.
He froze everything else. The billing module stopped. The new website stopped. Every morning his team called clinics, set them up and asked for payment.
On 15 March he walked in and put the card on the table. Twenty-three paying clinics. We didn't have to argue about opinions; the number decided it. That's why I don't like 'a few directions'. Pick one, give it a date, and let the date be honest."

qa.q: What was the deadline for the six-week test?
How might Sahil have felt walking in with twenty-three paying clinics?
qa.a: Sahil was probably relieved and proud, since the number settled the question without argument.

qa.q: Which choice in the story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Freezing all other work for the six weeks, because it let the whole team focus on getting clinics to pay for the reminder tool.

qa.q: How did the advisors experience the fixed report date?
qa.a: The advisors didn't have to argue about opinions; they could judge the result by one clear number.

grounding: It shows a team giving itself six weeks and one measure, twenty paying clinics for a reminder tool, freezing other work and reporting to advisors on a set date.

passage:
Payal and Tenzin wrote it on the whiteboard in their Kolkata office: "Six weeks. Twenty clinics paying for reminders. Advisors' meeting: 20 October." Everything else, the patient app and the billing screens, went into a folder labelled FROZEN.
The complication was the calendar. Week four was Durga Puja, when half the clinics in the city would shut and doctors would be at pandals, not answering sales calls. So they front-loaded: forty clinic visits in the first three weeks, setup done on the spot, trials ending just before the holidays.
By the end of week three they had eleven paying. During Puja, Tenzin sent gentle reminders to the rest, and Payal made a table of who had said "after the festival". In week five, nine more signed.
On 20 October they walked into the advisors' meeting with a single slide: 20.

qa.q: What went into the folder labelled FROZEN?
qa.a: The patient app and the billing screens.

qa.q: How did Payal feel about week four falling during Durga Puja?
qa.a: Payal was worried the festival would stall sales, which is why they packed the visits into the first three weeks.

qa.q: What made their plan work despite the festival?
qa.a: Front-loading clinic visits and setups into the first three weeks, then following up gently during the holidays.

qa.q: How might the advisors see the single slide?
qa.a: The advisors get a clear, honest answer on the one agreed measure, which makes the next decision easy.

grounding: It shows a team running a six-week test with one measure, twenty clinics paying for reminders, freezing other work and reporting to advisors on a fixed date despite a festival.
